title: SOUTERRAIN
description: Located at or near the bank bounding a field c 20m N of S its boundary. During the mid 60s a new main road was built, the junction of which lies very close to this field boundary. The area where souterrain is marked is not very accessible. Conversation with the owner revealed that souterrain had been open at the time of the road building (c 1965). He did not know whether or not the souterrain had been filled in when the road was built. See SM7 file for more details. An archaeological evaluation was carried out near the site of the souterrain, prior to construction of a laneway. A single test trench 40m x 2m was excavated along the proposed line of the lane. Several modern field drains were uncovered, but no trace of the souterrain or any other features of archaeological significance were found [CAF, Dec 06].

title: Souterrain
description: Located on a slight rise, with excellent views S-W-N, and the ground rising to E.  The remains of this souterrain were only partially visible when a small section caved in.  The top of the souterrain was located 1.2m below current ground level- although no capstone was in place (perhaps having also collapsed into the cavity).  The sides partially exposed indicated that the souterrain is aligned N-S.  No surviving trace of a bank or ditch for an associated rath could be identified at the time of site visit.  However, this is a suitable location for a rath.  A further souterrain is recorded from the OS Memoirs to be located approximately 270m NE.

description: This souterrain, set on a SE-facing slope, was rediscovered by the owner in 1983 when he removed a roofing slab. The almost linear creep runs NW upslope. Finds included sherds of coarse & fine souterrain ware, worked flints, charcoal & modern animal bones. The souterrain is currently closed, but may be reopened by the owner

description: On the E-facing brow of a ridge with fine views all round. The souterrain consists of a 4.5m length of collapsed & much robbed-out passage, aligned E/W. The W end of the souterrain is defined by a number of squared stones which form a set of rough steps leading down into the souterrain. The rubble in the collapsed passage all but obscures the surviving length of passage at the E end. It consists of 2 drystone walls set 0.7m apart, capped by a single large, flat slab. The passage appears to extend for a further 2m or so where it is either by further collapse or by the end of the souterrain. Two hawthorn bushes grow on top of it, the roots of which are causing most of the damage.

title: SOUTERRAIN
description: Parish: Donegore or Grange Of Nilteen?   On a S-facing hill slope with extensive views SE-S-SW. This souterrain, which is still open, is at the SE corner of a small, densely overgrown field. The opening, which appears to be a disturbed entrance at the W end of the souterrain is drystone built. The entrance descends into a passage leading off to E for c.3m before turning to NE where the souterrain constricts, beyond which the floor rises up into a possible chamber. The passage is built of on average 3 courses of large boulders roofed with huge flat slabs & is max.1.5m wide & 1.03m high. The constriction consists of 3 stones, 2 jambs & a lintel & is 0.45m wide x 0.42m high. The interior of the souterrain is very damp.

title: SOUTERRAIN
description: Barony: North East Liberties of Coleraine. This souterrain was found on the E side of Coleraine, outside the old walls & beside an ancient well. The souterrain was discovered & damaged during digging of foundations for a school hall in 1959. The entrance, which was broken down by the digger, is at the W end. From it the passage runs in a straight line for 25ft to E then curves NE of 10ft befort straightening up to E again. The floor is 8ft below surface level. The only finds were a couple of sherds of souterrain ware & a flint blade.

title: SOUTERRAIN
description: On the brow on an E-facing slope of a small hill with a very good view N, ESE of a mound [ant 008:020] & W of a farm. The owner pointed out the location of this souterrain, explaining that he had found it by plouging off a roofing stone many years ago to reveal a drystone built passage. He subsequently filled in the opening & there are now no visible remains of the souterrain. Mr.Todd did not enter the souterrin & had no information on its extent or components. There are 2 small quarries immediately N of the souterrain. There is no known tradition of an associated enclosure or mound.

title: SOUTERRAIN
description: An opening into this rock-cut souterrain is on the N side of the Magheramore road, in a steep S-facing slope of a bank, now overgrown. The only good view is to NE. The entrance is totally obscured by undergrowth & access into the souterrain is blocked by a slab laid across the opening. The souterrain is cut into basalt with a creep leading off to N; the blocking stone & some concrete in the opening prevent further observation. It is part of an Early Christian ecclesiastical settlement which includes a church & graveyard, a cross carved stone & a holy well [See Ant 008:009-011].

title: SOUTERRAIN
description: The entrance to this souterrain is at the base of a wall at the N of a large farmhouse.  It is 0.49m wide & 0.57m high & slopes down to a passage 0.53m wide x 0.9m high. This runs S for 2m then turns to SE for 1m & then runs S again. The 1st section of the passage is stone built & after that, it is completely rock cut & the height reduces to 0.53m. Further access was not attempted. According to a local farmer, his father entered the souterrain & got 30 yards before the air ran out. The entrance to the souterrain is temporarily closed with a stone.
